articles.text: Local restaurants limited again to serving takeout only On Saturday late afternoon, July 11, restaurant owners throughout Alameda County were suddenly notified to stop serving meals at their outdoor locations. The decision came less than two hours before dinner time on Saturday night, typically the busiest night of the week. The decision came when the California Office of Public Health added Alameda County to the state’s “monitoring list” because of a rise in COVID-19 cases. New restrictions include the rollback of restricted outdoor dining; restaurants may now serve only takeout and delivery. Though Alameda County’s Health Officer Order had allowed outdoor dining, under this stricter state guidance, all restaurants, wineries and bars throughout the county may only be open for drive-through or pick up and delivery options. “We are moving toward obtaining a variance from the state, and a letter of support for a variance is on the agenda for Tuesday [July 14] Board of Supervisors’ meeting,” said Neetu Blaram, Public Information Manager for the county’s Public Health Department. Alameda County hit pause on reopening on June 29 due to rising case rates and hospitalizations, but subsequently delayed plans to apply for a variance. Alameda County has the highest number of cases in the seven-county Bay Area. In recent days, seven states, including California, set new records for daily COVID-19 related deaths. This news comes nearly a month after outdoor dining launched in the region. As of press time, Alameda County remains one of only two counties in the state that has not yet applied for a variance. Imperial County, at the southern border of the state, is the other holdout. “It’s difficult to put a timeline [on this], because the first step in obtaining a variance would be the Board of Supervisors approving a letter of support, then the assumption would be that if they voted to approve the letter, then we can take the steps that are required to become a variance county,” Blaram told the Post. According to the Alameda County roadmap for reopening, outdoor dining was permitted on June 19, with restrictions. Each new development in reopening the county is contingent upon local COVID-19 indicators, at intervals of two and four weeks. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, in a press conference Monday afternoon, July 13, said, “We’re continuing to see hospitalizations rise and we continue to see an increase in the rate of positivity in the state. As a result, we are moving back into a ‘modification mode’ of our original stay-athome order, effective today.” Alameda County and 29 other counties fall under these stricter modifications. Gov. Newsom did not provide a guideline for when restaurants would be given authorization to reopen.

articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont School Board on June 25. Thank you for the discussion last evening and your work. I think that my comments and the comments of many others were misinterpreted yesterday, and I would like to clarify. Distancing learning must exactly duplicate 5 day per week in-person classes. This can easily be done by live-streaming the classes (just video on teacher, which would not be hard, as teachers will not be mobile to achieve distancing anyway) and sharing any in class materials (worksheets and handouts) via schoology. If this is not done, it would require much extra work for teachers to create separate content and the distancing students will get a lower quality of instruction, given the experience during this past spring. Piedmont does in class teaching well, so that should be the basis for distance learning. Having distance learning separate from a duplicate of in-class learning in the spring did not work. I have yet to find a single parent saying that distance learning in the spring was as good as in-class learning. Piedmont does in-class learning well, we just need to duplicate it for the distancing learning students. Having even one day per week that does not have in-class learning will result in that day of school being of lower quality. If distance learning in the spring that was different than in-class learning was woefully inadequate, and months of time was available to develop it, how would it be any different starting in just 1 and 1/2 months? As mentioned by school board members last night. Half of the kids could go in the morning, with the other half in the afternoon (or some other split by days over a two-week period of 10 days). This split would not be even for every class but should allow a reduction from a class size of 22 to 15 in all classes. Cohorts are not possible in high school. Exceptions would be with a change to a few tracks with the same classes. Cohorts with individualized schedules will not work in high school with very individualized class selection. It could work with several different choices (maybe 2 or 3) with all kids within those choices having the same classes. With this 2- or 3-track method, splitting the kids into two groups for AM or PM attendance would result in each class having 1/2 have kids in each. Numbers in each in class at less than 15, if the average class size were 22 (and still 15 with class sizes of 30). Need to establish full mask compliance. This can be done by suspending students for several days if they violate even once (they can distance learn for that suspension period). articles.text: Piedmont resident Peter Sherris received a rare honor on June 25, 2020., when Oakland Mayor Libby Schaff declared it Peter Sherris Day. It marked the end of his term as President the Rotary Club of Oakland, the third oldest in the U.S. Sherris’ resume of public service covers all spheres, from local to international. He has long been a Scoutmaster associated with Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop One, and has helped lead many backpacking trips in the high regions of the Sierra Nevada. Council Commissioner Rich Harms recalled Sherris’ impact on the Boy Scouts. “He was a good leader: he led by example with his formidable outdoor skills,” Harms said. “He took his troop of Piedmont Scouts on trips that they will remember for the rest of their lives. He led the troop on snow camping trips every winter and we were the only troop doing that at the time. We would build snow huts and sleep in those.” When not leading the Scouts in the Sierra or in the Yukon, Sherris worked his day job as a cardiologist and internist for 34 years with Kaiser Permanente. Through the Rotary Club he twice volunteered in the fight to eradicate malaria in Kenya. He returned to school to earn a Masters of Public Health at UC Berkeley. With Sherris at the helm of the Rotary Club this past year, Rotarians were prepared to undertake community service projects when COVID-19 hit. “Before 2020 started, Peter made sure we had consistent live streams of our meetings for members that couldn’t make it. articles.text: Justin Szasz, Piedmont’s CivicSpark Fellow and leader of the city’s Climate Plan for the past year, will be completing his 11-month program with the city at the end of July. His next stop will be a PhD in Sociology from the University of Oregon. A native of Santa Cruz, he obtained a Bachelor’s Degree in Social Studies from Harvard University in 2018, and for the past year has displayed considerable leadership with Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan, notably with the creation of a Climate Challenge. “I started [gaining interest] in climate change partway through college, I was primarily a Middle East studies major. By the time I was a junior, I was interested in what was then a very popular academic theory, that a drought connected to climate change played a role in sparking the Syrian civil war,” he explained. After some lengthy research, Szasz came to the conclusion that drought did play a role in the growth of existing problems. “An exacerbation of existing problems is in itself a real issue. So I became interested in the human impacts of climate change first, before I became interested in the determinants of climate change,” he said. From the fall 2018 to the next summer Szasz worked as a Research Assistant at the Harvard University Center for the Environment, studying the intersection of political economy and climate change. His studies followed how economic policies affect carbon emissions trajectories and how weather events connected to climate change interact with economic policies to affect populations. During that time, he applied for a CivicSpark Fellowship as Justin Szasz is leaving the Piedmont Planning Department to pursue a doctorate at the University of Oregon. a chance to learn how emissions reduction plans are created and implemented on a local level. He also took the opportunity as a chance to get involved in reducing California’s carbon emissions. CivicSpark is an AmeriCorps program in which fellows are matched with project partners throughout California, including the Central Coast, San Joaquin Valley, Los Angeles, San Diego, Sacramento, Sierra Nevada, and the San Francisco Bay Area. Fellows are matched with project partners to serve on at least one project, benefiting at least one local public agency. Szasz said that the Piedmont community was at the top of his list when considering where to work. articles.text: With caseload of more than 8,000, Alameda County added to State’s watchlist Three new cases of COVID- 19 were confirmed in Piedmont during the past seven days as cases in Alameda County soared above 8,000 as of Tuesday, July 14. It brings Piedmont’s total to 17 cases. One Piedmont case was reported last Wednesday, July 8, another was reported on Thursday, July 9, and a third was reported this week on Monday, July 13. Before the new cases in the past seven days, a new case was reported on July 3. Three cases were reported in May and 10 reported before April 13. Countywide, the caseload is now 8,321, an 11.6 percent increase from one week ago, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. In total, 152 people in the county have died due to COVID- 19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus, this year in the county. Alameda County is the hardest hit county in the San Francisco Bay Area. Santa Clara County now counts 6,542 cases and 167 total deaths. In Contra Costa County, the caseload is 5,023 and there have been 92 deaths. In San Francisco, the caseload is 4,640 and there have been 50 deaths. A total of 3,172 cases have been reported in Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County. Hayward now has a total of 1,277. Fremont has reported 425 cases, San Leandro has reported 419 cases and Berkeley has reported 278 cases. Due to its increasing numbers, Alameda County was placed on a statewide COVID-19 watchlist on Sunday, July 12. Counties on the watchlist cannot allow indoor activities like dining and museums. Those indoor activities were already prohibited by county orders. Outdoor restaurant dining was suddenly shut down by the County late Saturday afternoon, July 11. “Alameda County is experiencing a continued increase in reported COVID-19 cases in recent weeks, indicating elevated disease transmission,” the county said in a statement. “The magnitude of the change is above what would be expected as a result of the County‘s substantial expansion of testing.” Efforts to reopen more sectors of the economy in Alameda County were halted by officials at the end of June. In the announcement this week, county officials noted that although Alameda County had the most cases in the region, other counties in the area and statewide had higher case rates. California has seen a surge of cases in recent weeks and on Monday, July 13, the state ordered the closure of many indoor businesses, from restaurants to movie theaters. As of yesterday, there have been 336,508 total cases in California and 7,087 deaths. Piedmont’s annual Fourth of July Parade was canceled, although a socially distant, front yard decoration celebration took place. At a City Council meeting on Monday, July 6, City Administrator Sara Lillevand noted that the pandemic numbers were “not trending favorably” and predicted at that time that that Alameda County likely would be placed on the state’s watchlist. articles.text: Triple Threat Basketball Camp, operating camps for Piedmont’s Recreation Department for the 13th year, has moved its summer program outside to Hampton Park, rather than in the school gyms. The camps last three weeks and consist of pods of 12 players ages 6-12 playing three hours a day. The founder of the program, Tony Ferraro, wasn’t sure if any camps would be open this summer. “We had no intention of doing anything in Piedmont, but then got a call four weeks ago saying we can now do it outside,” he said. Camp registration filled up quickly like all the other in-person summer camps. Triple Threat had been operating at other locations since June 1. “We already had the protocols and the guide to reopen. The biggest difference with the Piedmont camp is that kids can actually play against each other and interact. Camps at our other locations have zero contact.” Players are screened for their temperature every day, and hands are frequently sanitized. Many kids show up with masks on, and some play with masks on. “I think they are trying to feel it out. articles.text: Science Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center This is a hands-on experiment our young scientists won’t soon forget. We all know the importance of thoroughly washing our hands, but how clean are our hands? How clean are these household and classroom items we touch multiple times a day? MATERIALS: • Enough slices of fresh, white bread for each item you’d like to test • 1 plastic sealable sandwich bag for each slice of bread that you’ll test • A control slice of bread that has not been touched (use gloves or clean tongs) • Whatever items are frequently touched in your home or classroom: • Clean hands: warm water and soap for 20 seconds • Clean hands: hand sanitizer • Dirty hands • Your face • Anything with a touch screen • Keyboard • TV remote or gaming controller • Door handle • Light switch • Your pillow PROCEDURE: 1. Using new gloves or clean tongs, remove 1 slice of fresh white bread and seal it into a plastic sandwich bag. Number and label the bag as Control (bag #1) 2. Wipe dry, clean hands that have been washed thoroughly for at least 20 seconds with soap and warm water on the next slice of bread. Number and label the bag as Clean hands- Soap and Warm Water (bag #2) 3. Continue to repeat this process for each surface you’d like to test. Make sure to correctly label and number each bag. 4. Leave the sealed bags with their labels on a table or counter for up to one month. 5. Make predictions about which slices of bread will grow the most mold. Which slices will get moldy the fastest? Why? Find more activities and at-home experiments on Chabot’s Learning Launchpad at chabotspace.org. Be sure to share your observations with us on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter @chabotspace. We all know the importance of thoroughly washing our hands, but how clean are our hands? How clean are these household and classroom items we touch multiple times a day? MATERIALS: • Enough slices of fresh, white bread for each item you’d like to test • 1 plastic sealable sandwich bag for each slice of bread that you’ll test • A control slice of bread that has not been touched (use gloves or clean tongs) • Whatever items are frequently touched in your home or classroom: • Clean hands: warm water and soap for 20 seconds • Clean hands: hand sanitizer • Dirty hands • Your face • Anything with a touch screen • Keyboard • TV remote or gaming controller • Door handle • Light switch • Your pillow PROCEDURE: 1. Using new gloves or clean tongs, remove 1 slice of fresh white bread and seal it into a plastic sandwich bag. Number and label the bag as Control (bag #1) 2. articles.text: –John Savage Piedmont High Science Teacher Parents and families involved with Piedmont Makers have led a fundraising campaign to finish the designated engineering lab in the new 3-story STEAM classroom building on the site of the former high school theater. The STEAM building, set for completion in four weeks, will house science, technology, art, engineering and mathematics classes. The capstone of the $30 million building is expected to be an engineering lab, long touted as the school’s future. But the project has come up short. The cost to outfit the engineering lab was estimated at $420,000. That work appears not to have been included in the overall cost of the building. The Piedmont Makers organization leaped to the rescue, launching a campaign to raise $420,000. As of a week ago, $320,000 had been raised, but the outfitting of the lab is not expected to be completed until late January 2021 at the start of the second semester. At a presentation at the July 7 school board meeting, PHS Principal Adam Littlefield said, “We’re still creating the vision for the use of the engineering lab, but at this point it includes project-based learning integrated into curriculum, and really a space to build things.” There will be a focus on engineering and technology-based activities, Littlefield continued, with a goal to allow students to design and manufacture using state-of-the art equipment. A “library-like” resource center, with software driven tools and traditional manual tools, is included in the vision. Littlefield added that he would like to see the lab available for community members beyond students and district staff, clearing the way for the space to be utilized by members of the Piedmont Makers. “The STEAM building, including the engineering lab, would be open to community groups, as would the facilities within PUSD,” said Littlefield. Piedmont Makers, a nonprofit founded in 2014, helped convert the Piedmont Middle School woodshop to a robotics and maker space. It sponsors more than 30 teams in the Youth Robotics League. In the first quarter of this year, Piedmont Makers worked with Supt. Randy Booker and Littlefield to discuss outfitting the engineering lab, and then worked with Facilities Director Pete Palmer to develop a layout and an equipment list. Highlander Robotics worked with several non-profits to obtain plastic, and then cut and designed into personal protective equipment (PPE) for nurses, back in March when there was a significant shortage. “PPE is a simple project and could be translated to a project that the class or community could work on. It’s a great way to connect the community to the STEAM lab,” said Charlie Lambert. Sally Aldridge is leading the fundraising campaign to outfit the lab. “We started this effort quite a while ago, before COVID, and were fortunate enough to get some large anchor donors on board early,” she said. Maker Space created a detailed three-year operating budget of $420,000, including district-certified lab staff. “This budget is over and above the H1 plans, so there’s no need to dip into any existing funds,” Aldridge said. “We think of this plan much like the Wellness Center at the high school, which started with outside donations.” A future goal is to raise $50,000 from the community and $50,000 to be matched by an anonymous donor. To recognize these donors, a Donor Wall will be placed in the hallway outside the lab. “The school budget is so tight, and I appreciate the thoughtfulness put [into this budget], and thinking through relieving pressure from the district budget,” school board member Cory Smegal said. articles.text: Right now, you probably are sobbing in your room because you missed out on your Paris trip, or how you couldn’t go to Greece. It’s okay. I was supposed to go to Hawaii with my family, but since COVID hit and Hawaii closed its doors for tourists, we weren’t able to go. To my surprise, we quickly found a solution. We booked a hotel in Pismo Beach and in Yosemite - a whole week of vacation! I was so excited to finally get out of my house for longer than an hour. In less than a week we were packed and ready to go to Pismo Beach, near San Luis Obispo. At first, I was a bit shocked because nobody was wearing a mask. There were so many people it looked like summer in Disney World, not DisneyLand, folks, But don’t get me wrong, I loved Pismo Beach, although it has a few faults. For those of you who haven’t gone on vacation during the quarantine, not much has changed, except that you have to wear a mask and observe social distancing. Hotel restaurants are mostly takeout. My sister and I went down to the beach and as soon we arrived. It was like Hawaii. The sand at Pismo is so white and soft. The water was still cold but, not as cold as in Northern California, especially Point Reyes. Walking down the beach was a workout because walking on sand is not easy when you’re walking on a shifting surface and it’s hot. I didn’t last 20 minutes. Some people at our hotel were quite self-absorbed. There was a family that took up three outdoor fireplaces and just left their stuff on the chairs and left. That made it kind of touch for other people who were freezing from sitting by the comfort of a warm fire (my family included). Quite rude, but then nobody asked me. After spending three days in Pismo Beach we drove to Yosemite, a four-hour trip. In that time, it was amazing to see the coastal terrain turn into mountains with lush forests. Initially we stayed at the Pines Resort at Bass Lake, which was like one small town. There were restaurants, convenience stores, even a post office. The housing units were called chalets, each with an individual name. Ours was the “Sunrise Chalet”, with a view of the hills and the lake. One of the perks at this resort was that we could rent boats – plus the fact that we were only 13 miles from Yosemite. After settling in, we went outside to explore the resort. We were alerted by an employee in a golf cart that there was a bear running loose through the area. When I asked her whether this happened often, she said, “You’re in the mountains, sweetheart,” I almost died from laughter. Kind of like “You’re not in Kansas, Anymore.” The next day we drove to the park. On our way we made jokes about how when you get to Yosemite it’s supposed to be a spiritual awakening. But when we came out of the tunnel we were stunned. Mountains jutting out from the side. Bridalveil Falls in the distance. The Merced River winding through the trees. It was spectacular. After taking many pictures, we drove into the Valley, and at some point we realized that we had lost the permit that let us in the park, So we put a note that said “lost” (it, not us), and hoped for the best. Walking under the towering redwoods and oaks was an amazing experience. Unlike in Pismo, many people were wearing masks, which was comforting. We wanted to go up to MIrror Lake but didn’t find the trail entrance. Instead we took the Mist Trail to Vernal Falls. When I tell you it was hard, you do not understand unless you yourself have attempted this hike. I’m not kidding, it just went up and up, and it was hot. But we kept our masks on the whole time. But in the end, the torturous hike was well worth it. The thundering falls blocked out sound and all you could see was the beauty of this massive waterfall. What utterly confused me was seeing people in their 60s and 70s and children walking on the steep trail on the way back down like it was flat. Maybe there is something wrong with us. Who knows? After a long day at Yosemite we went to Glacier Point, watched the gorgeous sunset and drove back to Bass Lake. The next day we could barely move, but nonetheless got up because we had reserved a boat for a couple of hours. There is something you need to know: At Bass Lake there are different cliques of teenagers. Makenna Thiel, an incoming Piedmont High senior and the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2018, has officially committed to the University of California tennis program in Berkeley. “I grew up going to every Cal men’s basketball game with my family. When I started looking into each school, I found that Cal was perfect in every way for me. It has a great balance between athletics and academics. “I am grateful for this opportunity,” said Thiel. Thiel said her decision came down to Cal and USC, but her familiarity with Berkeley and the Golden Bears ultimately won her over. “It was always a dream of mine to stay in the Pac 12. I feel like a part of the team already. I’ve hit with some of them in the past and met a few at tournaments, so I feel already close with some of the girls already. “That was a huge draw; it’s great to know people where I’m going,” she added. Thiel will be playing under head coach Amanda Augustus and assistant Zach Warren, who helped lead the school to the second round of the 2019 NCAA Championships. “Both Amanda and Zach are great coaches. I’ve played on the Cal courts a few times and I’d see them at tournaments. I noticed that I played better when they watched me; I realized that I was already comfortable in their presence despite not knowing them on a personal level yet,” said Thiel. Thiel is a four-star recruit and has continuously been ranked among the top prospects in the state. She’s competed in top-level regional tournaments since her pre-teen years and remains a premier competitor. She helps solidify the Cal tennis program’s best recruiting class of all time, giving Augustus and Warren possibly their best shot at topping archrival and back-to-back NCAA champs, Stanford. Alongside Thiel as freshmen will be five-star recruit Cami Brown of Irvine, Canadian champion Jada Bui, and Hannah Viller Moller of Denmark. “We worked very hard to bring in a group we feel includes outstanding young women who are great fits at Cal athletically and academically. I believe this is the highest rated recruiting class in program history,” said Augustus. “In combination with the class we brought in this past year and with our veteran players, we’re really excited about the upcoming 2020- 21 season,” he added. Thiel’s time on Piedmont High’s tennis team was only two years, but she made it count. She won all but one match in over 20 appearances and was named the Western Alameda County Conference’s MVP for the fall of 2017 and 2018. She won the Div. 1 NCS doubles’ championship with Lauren Young. Thiel was part of Piedmont’s run of five consecutive Division 2 North Coast Section Team Championships, which started with her older sister, Kaelli Thiel, in 2013. “I remember Makenna at 11-years old saying she wants to play professional tennis, which was rare for someone at that age,” recalled former PHS tennis coach and Hall of Fame inductee. “She always had that John McEnroe attitude and is a fierce player.” “Even as a fifth grader Makenna would always came to our matches. Haas is a great business school.” Makenna Thiel was named Athlete of the Year by the Piedmont Post in 2019, and Freshman of the Year in 2018.

articles.text: With the summer months rolling along, athletes at Piedmont High face an unconventional offseason ahead of the fall. You may see some members of the girls’ cross-country team working on their mileage on runs around town. The entire team is taking part in the Athletes as Leaders’ program with coach Jeanine Holmlund. The program provides a weekly topic and a video to watch, discuss and reflect on in terms of values. “Within our group we give each student a platform to discover and articulate her thoughts. At the very least, we are sharing our feelings and becoming a tighter group through this experience,” said Holmlund. The program enables student-athletes to deal with issues like social awareness, civil rights, mental health and understanding societal stereotypes. It also aids teenagers toward processing personal matters like self-image positivity and developing healthy relationships. “I want the girls to recognize they are more than athletes and students. I want them to believe in themselves and have confidence in their ideas as they move forward and out of high school. Our running programs offer coping skills and life skills, a place to reflect and to grow as individuals,” explained Holmlund. Aya Troyer embarks on her senior campaign with some familiar faces around her, including Adri McAullife, Mara Lovric, Molly McWeeny, Valerie Xiong, Katie Korn, and the Posts’ Sophomore of the Year, Ellie Black. Troyer will eb a four-year varsity runner. “Aya Troyer, Katie Korn and Valerie Xiong have joined. They are running over 35 miles a week and are a really committed group,” added Holmlund. It will be the first time in four years that the team has not had Sofia Zalewski as a team leader. A record-setting runner, she finished her high school career as Valedictorian and will be attending Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburg. Holmlund is hopeful that the Athletes as Leaders program facilitates a leader-mentality going into the fall. “We have a committed girls’ team. When looking ahead to the fall, the NFHS classified cross country as a “low risk” sport if athletes are given staggered starts—meaning racers would start individually instead of the traditional herd of runners at the starting line. articles.text: Photo by Todd Marshburn Will there be sports at Witter Field this fall? The CIF’s decision on sports comes on July 20. Student-athletes, coaches, parents, and high school sports supporters are all intently waiting for Monday, July 20, when the California Interscholastic Federation – the governing body for high school sports in the stet – has said it will announce plans for fall sports – if, when and how they will take place. On June 10, the CIF announced its two phases toward safely re-opening with some training guidelines and a July 20 deadline for the specifics. In May, the National Federation of State High School Associations and Sports Medicine Advisory Committee released its classifications for sports deemed “High Risk” to “Low Risk”. • High Risk: Wrestling, football, boys’ lacrosse, competitive cheer, and dance. • Moderate Risk: Basketball, volleyball, baseball, softball, soccer, water polo, gymnastics, ice hockey, field hockey, tennis, swimming relays, pole vault, high jump, long jump, girls lacrosse, crew with two or more rowers, 7 on 7 football. • Low Risk: Individual running events, throwing events (javelin, shot put, discus), individual swimming, golf, weightlifting, alpine skiing, sideline cheer, single sculling, and cross country running with staggered starts. The NFSH marked several “Moderate Risk” sports could be considered “Low Risk” with appropriate cleaning of equipment and athletes using masks, including volleyball, baseball, softball, gymnastics, tennis, pole vault, high jump, and long jump. Coaches at Piedmont High have confirmed that as of now, everything is up in the air. Cross country coach Jeanine Holmlund said, “I don’t expect to know anything sooner. NCS, WACC and Piedmont will be making decisions within the CIF’s framework.” Water polo coach John Savage said, “I haven’t heard anything else.” “The CIF has been very quiet about their decision,” commented football coach Jerome Johnson. Many coaches at Piedmont have indicated that they’d be “surprised” by a fall season, giving a dark cloud over the July 20 announcement date. Former coach Neil Rothenberg joked that he considered retiring after the 2014 championship win, but Thiel convinced him to stay until she graduated. He said, “OK, but only if you play Division 1singes as a senior.” She did. She won, and the rest is history. “That run was pretty amazing when we started with Kaelli. I’ve always been proud of all the teams, but that whole run was really special,” said Rothenberg. Kaelli Thiel graduated in 2015 as one of the most decorated PHS tennis player of all time. She finished with a four-year overall record of 94-10 and won both the Div. 1 and Div. 2 North Coast Section singles championships. Following Rothenberg’s retirement in 2015, Jim Landes took over the program. In 2016 and gained two more NCS championship wins over Branson prior to the 2018 vacated year due to the Butte County fire pollution. The 2016 team featured Angela Huang as a sophomore winning the Division 2 NCS singles title and completed its 18th consecutive undefeated league championship season. 14 Wednesday, July 15, 2020 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 13th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. JUKKA VALKONEN Triathlon Piedmont High Class of 1985 Cal State East Bay Class of 1991 Piedmont’s Jukka Valkonen is a member of the US National Team as a triathlete. He currently is training for the USAT Off-road Triathlon National Championships in September. A professional trainer and physical health expert, Valkonen is working as the Chief Health Officer for the largest AI tech-enabled medical practice that is aiding with the global impact of COVID-19. He shares an important message regarding athletes, teams, and being safe during the global pandemic. What is your workout program this summer? With COVID19, the focus has been keeping the mind, body and spirit healthy. Early in the year and pandemic, I reminded my fellow athletes we are going to be in a storm and as humans we are designed to get out of the rain and hunker down. That meant keep the body healthy but not stressed. Training for competition puts one right on the thin line of illness and race readiness. My program has been focused on a balance of endurance, power and technique work all while having fun and not stressing. I’m not training any less, but I’m also not stressing over a regimen and weight. What are your fitness goals for the summer? The focus is being resilient. Right now, my National Championships in September hasn’t been cancelled, so that’s the focus without stressing the body. How are you measuring your development? I have many years of benchmark data and also know what I need to accomplish in order to achieve my competition goals. For fun, I unofficially came close to matching the world record in the Murph, an exercise test common in CrossFit and many sports. I’m currently focused on the Abbate, which at the competition level weight is still a little out of my reach. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I work on my own and with a couple of racing buddies. I’ve been a pro sports trainer so I know what I need to do. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Unofficially close to matching the world record in the Murph, and am at an elite level with the Abbate. I also did possibly the first ever Swim/Run from Emeryville to Richmond. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? As a rugby coach, I always say to the athletes and parents: the main two objectives are safety and fun. COVID has, for now, tremendously changed sports. Super pros, Olympians, college and HS athletes are testing positive. All it takes is one teammate to be irresponsible. I see way too many kids (and adults) not heeding public health requirements, especially with masks. While the team that gets infected may not have very sick athletes, not only do they put others at risk, but they put their opportunity to play their sport at risk. We aren’t in the same boat, but we are in the same storm. Sasha Liu, PHS Class of 2019, recently finished her freshman year at Brown University as a member of the swim team. SASHA LIU Swimming ress with my times in practice. I have noticed my repeats improve in the last month, which is very motivating. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? In the time pools were closed, Elie Cole [former All-American lacrosse athlete] and I would go on long walks and we were able to get up to 15 miles walking from Lafayette to Walnut Creek. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? Completing my freshman year at Brown. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Try to find the positives in what you’re doing. The break I had from swimming gave me perspective on things I had taken for granted. articles.text: For this week’s hike, we return to Marin County and its landmark, Mt. Tamalpais, to seek out some views and a steady incline for an adequate lower-body workout. After many trails were closed in March at the start of the pandemic, county officials declared Mt. Tam re-opened for the public last month for hikers. For this trip, we start at Mt. Tam’s Quarry Parking Lot heading 1.5 miles down the Rock Spring Trail until intersecting with the historic West Point Inn. Our ascent starts from there, trekking two miles up to the East Peak, 2.4 miles to the opposite West Peak, and 1.2 miles back to the car. Once again, the spread of COVID-19 is still a concern for everyone. If you go out, do it responsibly. Here are our guidelines for hiking amidst the virus: • Research parking or trail restrictions for whatever park you choose. • Be mindful. Always bring a face cover of some sort. • The earlier the better. Trails are most trafficked past noon. • Find lesser used trailheads. Hiking on weekdays provides less traffic. • Go solo or plus-one. No large groups. To my surprise, there were just two other cars at the Mt. Tamalpais Quarry Lot upon my arrival after driving past many other lots filled to capacity. It’s been some time since our last trip to Mt. Tam when we visited Cataract Creek, an often-visited site. The 1.5 miles trip on the Rock Spring Trail was mostly level and downhill toward the West Point Inn with continuously improving views of San Francisco, the Marin Headlands, Sausalito, and the Pacific Ocean below. On your way to the West Point Inn, you’ll go through groves of California Bay Laurel trees and a stretch of a serpentine rock formation with a striking green hue. The West Point Inn, although closed due to COVID-19, has accommodated visitors since 1904 when it was a stopping point on the Mill Valley and Mt. Tamalpais Scenic Railway. From there, you’ll travel along the backside of the Inn on the Old Railroad Grade to East Ridgecrest Boulevard toward the East Peak’s parking lot. Gaining some 750 feet in elevation, you’ll reach the Gardner Fire Lookout for another sweeping view of the North Bay. It’s worth mentioning that the East Peak is among the most popular destinations of Mt. Tam, meaning you’ll be passing by lots of people just there for a quick view. I observed 17 people in the 3.5 miles toward the East Peak. On the walk up to Gardner Lookout, however, there were more than 30 people from the parking lot. Leaving the crowd, we traveled 2.4 miles down East Ridgecrest toward the West Peak – a much less visited and less developed area. I saw no other hikers on my walk down the boulevard. The walk toward the peak continued, with stellar views of San Francisco and the Marin Headlands, while gaining another 450 feet of elevation. West Peak is being restored and is fenced off. A large radio toward sits on the hill, but aside of a glimpse of the A view of the empty parking lot at the Quarry Lot, a. great starting point to avoid crowds. The Gardner Lookout point was created in 1937 and remains a popular destination.

articles.text: Cellist Gabriel Martins Musaics of the Bay is offering another presentation from its “Stay-at-home Symposium” series. The fourth in the series, released last week, is a solo cello piece by composer Milad Yousufi and performed by Gabriel Martins. The work, titled “Mystery,” is a work inspired by a photograph by Dale Carter called “Ridges in Sand 1.” The photograph was, in turn, inspired by the paintings of Mark Rothko. “There is a gentle sense of serenity and contemplation in [Rothko’s] paintings that I attempted to capture in this series,” Carter told Musaics of the Bay founder Audrey Vardanega. “Like Rothko, I took a meditative approach to this piece, with the soft color scheme. My main focus, though, was on capturing those fleeting, beautiful moments in nature when it reveals itself.” The Stay-at-home Symposium is a community collaboration and series of broadcasts featuring music premieres based on the creativity of community members – composers, performers, and artists of all types. “We believe in the power of classical music to enrich and heal us, especially in these uncertain times,” Vardanega said. articles.text: As the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra ensemble shelters in place, Music Director Ben Simon has put his time in quarantine to good use by launching the “Simon Says Show.” In the first episode, Simon shares two examples of famous composers stealing from “our planet’s greatest musicians: the birds.” He explores how birdsongs made their way into classical works by Vivaldi and Beethoven. Simon provides some historical background to these two works, and explains how the music was influenced by birdsong, quoting Vivaldi’s own words. Simon breaks up the short explanation with some musical humor, for which he is well known (and well loved): “What does a lawsuit and a viola have in common? Everyone is relieved when the case is closed.” Watch Ben Simon’s first episode of the Simon Says Show on YouTube by visiting https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=8Z_lT7cdwF8&feature=emb_title. articles.text: A scene from Capernaum Movie review by Chris Honoré The title Capernaum comes from French literature and means chaos. And indeed, chaos is the essence of this film, permeating the narrative with a bleakness that is unrelenting. The story, however, is wondrous, and is testimony to the resilience of the human spirit. If there is beauty and hope in Capernaum it is revealed through a 12-year-old boy, Zain (Zain Al Refeea). It’s from Zain’s point of view that we are introduced to the squalid, desperately mean streets of Beirut. Everywhere and everything conveys this. The flatroofed, square, crumbling houses and shops, stacked one on top of the other are barely habitable. Everyone has a hustle, and if Zain is to survive, he must make his way, using all the street smarts he can muster. He endures the snarls and slaps and abuse from his mother and father (Kawthar Al Haddad and Fadi Kamel Youseef), both grifters and drug dealers, resisting and ignoring their threats, all the while working the streets and watching other kids going to and from school. There is only one person he cares about, truly loves, and that is his sister, Sahar (Cedra Izam), one year younger. He is fearful, even desperate, that his parents do not discover that she is on the cusp of her menarche, lest she be sold to their landlord’s son as part of a forced marriage bargain. When he learns that that is what they have done, in a rage, he runs away. And so begins act two in which he is befriended by a young Ethiopian woman, Rahil (Yordanos Shiferaw), who has a small child. She is an undocumented refugee. Zain becomes the babysitter while Rahil goes to work. It is a responsibility he takes most seriously, his courage and empathy evident, his concern for the small boy constant. But then events change everything. Capernaum has been nominated for Best Foreign Film, and has a documentary feel about it. It is a searing close up, a brutal window through which we see a brittle humanity in granular detail. Chaos defines everything, until it doesn’t. The last image on the screen is of a smiling Zain. Capernaum. Directed by Nadine Labaki. In Arabic with English subtitles. Starring Zain Al Rafeea, Yordanos Shiferaw and Cedra Izzam. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated R. Zain Al Rafeea in a scene from Capernaum.
articles.title: Capernaum – nominated for Best Foreign Film of 2018

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honore’ Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood is not surprisingly an off-center homage to, well, Hollywood. The year is 1969. The film glows with SoCal sunshine, blue skies, prologue traffic with airplane-size cars, and is more introspective than director Quentin Tarantino’s previous oeuvre. I’ve always been ambivalent about his movies (Pulp Fiction was made 25 years ago), yet interested, maybe even captivated, by their quirky plots and strong characters. Still, I’ve bridled at what has always seemed to me to be gratuitous, over-the-top violence and sideways action. The Hateful Eight is a good example. I knew nothing about the movie upon entering, and had not seen the trailer if there was one. I only knew that Brad Pitt and Leonardo DiCaprio starred in what, at first glance, seemed a buddy movie. For much of act one I worked at giving the movie a chance as it moseyed from one digression to the next as the Pitt and DiCaprio characters, Cliff Booth and Rick Dalton, were introduced. Rick is a fading TV star who appeared just long enough in a western series titled Bounty Law to give him name recognition and offers of Movie of the Week guest gigs as villainous characters. Cliff was Rick’s stunt double in the TV series and has remained his friend and salaried assistant/ go-fer who only works when Rick does. The narrative focuses on these two men, both aging-out of mainstream Hollywood and both reacting in decidedly different ways. Rick is a bundle of insecurity in the grip of a tormenting angst, which he buffers with alcohol. In one scene, on a movie set and in his trailer, he berates himself for missing his lines, looking in a mirror threatening to take a gun to his head if he doesn’t pull it together. Cliff, in contrast, takes life as it comes, is studiously content to support Rick, keeping him and his fragile self-confidence barely moving forward and running errands as needed. Gradually, the film engages, cutting back and forth from Rick’s latest villain gig to Cliff hanging out, or at home in his trailer with his dog. While both now work at the edges of the industry, there’s still work to be had. The story’s through line is the headline-grabbing murder that occurred in August of 1969. A sometimes actress Sharon Tate and others are killed by the Manson Family, a group of psychotic followers of Charles Manson, perpetrators of what later became known as the Tate-LaBianca murders. But consider the title of the movie: Once Upon a Time…. This is a Tarantino fantasy, viewed through the prism of pop culture and Hollywood road signs, framing how tragic events might’ve been, could’ve been, if only. In Act II, Tarantino seems to find a nice rhythm, crafting some excellent, very watchable scenes. One captures Tate (Margot Robbie), a second tier movie star married to director Roman Polanski (Rosemary’s Baby), out running errands. She goes into a movie theater to watch herself in a film. The camera holds on her face, a smile touching her eyes as the audience reacts to her scenes. It’s a tender moment, though a bit ominous given what has been so indirectly foreshadowed. There is also a vignette that is both wonderful and foreboding when Cliff picks up a young hippy girl hitchhiking (Margaret Qualley). She tells him she lives with her friends at the Spahn Ranch and begins to give him directions. He, however, knows the way since it’s been a familiar location for westerns. It’ is now where a cohort of hippies is living/squatting. When Cliff and the girl arrive, he is not greeted with flower power, or a groovy vibe. Standing on the front porches are feral young women – ranch denizens, suspicious and unwelcoming. Cliff knows that the ranch is owned by a cantankerous, partially blind geezer, George Spahn (Bruce Dern). He insists on saying hello to him, just to see that all is well. There is is a long, harrowing scene as Cliff tries to judge George’s well-being. Though not quite satisfied, he leaves, taking a slow walk back to his car, past the hostile gathering of hippie women. What shouldn’t surprise, given Tarantino’s predilection for reactionary violence, is that he turns the Hollywood hippies into foils. In one scene, Rick, who is drunk, hearing a car entering his private cul-de-sac walks out to the street while holding a blender of margaritas and in a scatological rant tells the hippie driver and his passengers to back up and get out. Tarantino skips all the counterculture good feeling gestalt of the 60s, choosing instead to portray them as deranged cultists. Which, hewing to a semblance of history, the Manson clan was, though not representative. This scene leads to the harrowing climax of the film, one that is breathtakingly outrageous, pure Tarantino, yet fits into the farrago of myth and fact that has always permeated Hollywood. Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood. Directed by Quentin Tarantino. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Brad Pitt and Margot Robbie. 2 hrs., 39 min. Rated R. Reprinted from Piedmont Post on August 7, 2019

articles.text: A scene from Spielberg’s movie, The BFG. Movie review by Chris Honoré The BFG (Big Friendly Giant), based on Roald Dahl’s children’s book, proves to be a soft, beautifully imagined film that captures the power of enchantment that only film can fully create, especially when crafted by a director with the skill of Steven Spielberg. Visually, it is wondrous to behold. With the aid of computer graphics, Mark Ryance (from Bridge of Spies) is transformed into an enormous giant whose face is deeply creased by smiles, possesses enormous ears, and eyes that capture the sparkle and joy of his job. He’s Merlin, an alchemist, a gentle soul who lives in an out-ofplumb house. He visits, beneath a canopy of stars, the dream tree where he captures small whizzing stars and dreams (not unlike Tinkerbell) and bottles them for later. It is a stunning scene, breathtaking in all aspects. And what does he do with those glowing, luminous stars? At night, when all are sleeping, BFG goes forth from giant land, stealthily visiting the city, and with his trumpet-like, spiraling horn that has attached a bottle of captured dreams, he blows them, one at a time, into the mouths of kids and adults. It’s on one such outing that he is spotted by 10-year-old Sophie (Ruby Barnhill), a plucky, precocious orphan who climbs out of bed and stands on a narrow balcony staring at this enormous creature in complete disbelief. Afraid that she will reveal his presence, he kidnaps her and takes her back to his digs in Giant Land. His home is a marvelous place filled with inventions and bottled dreams, each container glowing and carefully labeled. Sophie is mere inches tall by comparison and suddenly finds herself in a world of huge items, to include the strange talking conjurer of dreams, the BFG. If there is a dark side to The BFG, it’s the nine stupendously massive dunderhead giants who live near BFG. They also happen to be carnivores of “human beans” (or just “beans”). Apparently they’ve been taking small children and consuming them and would love to find Sophie for the same reason. Hence their visit to BFG’s cavern-like home. BFG, of course, is desperate to keep her hidden among the jars and bowls set on the shelves and the tables, lest her fate follow that of the other children. However, these really big giants (far taller than BFG, called “Runt” by the crew) never seem to present a serious threat to Sophie. Spielberg, and his screenwriter, the late Melissa Mathison (famous for E.T.) are content to keep Sophie out of any real jeopardy, meaning the sense of excitement never rises to any real breathtaking level. And so there’s a sense of brief longueur in act two. Things don’t really gain any real momentum until act three when Sophie goes to the Queen of England (Penelope Wilton) and most humbly asks for her help with the nine giants. After introducing her to BFG, of course. For kids watching this film, the question of whether there is enough story in The BFG to stand alone, absent the many joyous and visually captivating scene is not relevant. The answer, aimed at the adults who will be sprinkled throughout the audience is, well, sort of. But it’s not a story in which the stakes seem precariously high. In essence, the nine giants are cannibals who relish feasting on “beans.” Shudder. But in some strange way they seem rather harmless. Instead, The BFG is testimony to Spielberg’s love of the magic that film can create on a grand scale. Today, given the astonishing technology available to filmmakers, there is nothing imagined that cannot be created, meaning a story can transcend all limitations that were once thought of as constraints. From an adult point of view, I’m not sure that Dahl’s 1982 book was ever well suited to be made into a movie; however, what is clear is that in The BFG, Spielberg has made a wondrous attempt. Kids will love it. When it concluded, they clapped. Tangentially, I’ve always believed that one of his best children’s movies – well, quasi-children’s movies – is The Empire of the Sun, in which the stakes are enormous for a young boy struggling to survive at a POW camp during World War II. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The character “Astro Boy” was created in 1951 by the celebrated animator of Japanese manga (comic books) and anime (movie and television animation), Osamu Tezuka. In the 1960s, Astro, originally known as Tetsuwan Atomu (Mighty Atom), appeared in a popular television show, viewed in more than 40 countries. Now Astro makes his debut in a feature film. For children today, Astro Boy will be new and fresh. They will be captivated by the story and the nonstop action. This first installment (others will likely follow) explains how a young boy, Toby (Freddy Highmore), is killed in an experiment conducted by his scientist father, Dr. Tenma (Nicolas Cage). Wracked with grief and guilt, Tenma creates an exact replica of his son, a small android, giving him all of Toby’s memories and a heart of “blue power” which makes the boy superhuman. He can fly, has x-ray vision, amazing strength, and rockets in his shoes and hands. At first unaware he’s a robot, Astro sets out to find his place in the world, meaning Metro City, an urban island hovering above earth which has been turned into a dumpsite for outdated robots and broken machinery. After being rejected by his father, who cannot accept that he’s a robot, Astro goes to earth and meets a group of kids, orphans from Metro City and all his own age. These discarded kids have no families. They are, however, human and Astro is reluctant to disclose that he is not. The kids long for Astro’s powers and he longs for their humanity. He also grieves for the loss of his father. There’s an evil Mayor of Metro City (Donald Sutherland) who covets Astro’s “blue power,” and a duplicitous hustler named Hamegg (Nathan Lane) who wants only to use Astro. It’s a long journey back to the arms of his father. While the story brings to mind Transformers and even Pinocchio, kids will find Astro appealing and will look forward to The Return of Astro Boy. Astro Boy. Animated. With the voices of Nicolas Cage, Freddie Highmore, Nathan Lane, Kristen Bell and Bill Nighy. Directed by David Bowers. Rated PG. Reprinted from Piedmont Post on October 28, 2009.

articles.text: If you have kids pacing back and forth with that “there’s nothing to do” look in their eyes, I would suggest that you convince them to do a deep dive into the world of animation. Think of it as a tutorial, beginning with the proliferation of the animated films of Hayao Miyazaki. A world-renowned Japanese animator, filmmaker, screenwriter, author, and manga artist (Japanese comic books), he strongly influenced Pixar and Disney in the U.S. in their storytelling and art of animation. Miyazaki began what has been an extraordinary career in 1963, immersing himself in the world of manga and film animation (anime), with hand drawn and later computer-generated animation originating in Japan. He co-founded Studio Ghibli in 1985 where he and fellow animators found critical and commercial success throughout the world with the films Castle in the Sky, My Neighbor Totoro and the hugely successful Princess Mononoke (released in 1997). He went on to win an Oscar at the Academy Awards in 2001 for the animated feature, Spirited Away. Hayao Miyazaki, Japan’s world-famous animator and founder of Studio Ghibli, who strongly influenced both Pixar and Disney in the U.S. Using colorful graphics, vibrant characters, and fantastical themes, which thread through films such as Kiki’a Delivery Service, The Wind Rises, Spirited Away, Nausica of the Valley, Ponyo and From Up on Poppy Hill, Miyazaki has explored humanity’s relationship with nature and technology as well as capturing the perpetual sense of wonder inherent in young people. In his work he has also examined the obstacles encountered as one tries to maintain a pacifist ethic in a violent world, while also examining themes that touch on love, family and feminism. Many of his protagonists are young women, never objectified, who struggle with the complexities inherent to their gender. In 2012, Miyazaki was named a Person of Cultural Merit for his cultural contributions, and, in 2014, he received the Academy’s honorary award for his impact on animation and cinema worldwide. articles.text: Arturo Toscanini was the greatest orchestra conductor of his time. He achieved the highest quality performances from his orchestras with an uncontrolled temper that rivaled the explosion of Krakatoa. Many of his rehearsals were recorded. These document the eruptions which seem to be over absolutely insignificant things. Yelling and screaming and insults were his modus operandi. He was unbelievably severe with his musicians. He could also be brutal with his own mistakes. In order to placate him and put him in a good mood, his musicians presented him with a very expensive gold-encased pocket watch. It lasted less than one rehearsal. His temper flared and he took out that very expensive watch, flinging it to the ground and breaking it to smithereens. His musicians learned their lesson. They gave him another watch. This time it was a cheap one… which he smashed during the very next rehearsal. One time, Toscanini yelled at a musician telling him to play mezzo forte. They played the passage again, but the musician played exactly the same way the second time. Toscanini yelled even louder. “I told you to play mezzo forte!” The musician looked blandly at the maestro and calmly said, “Maestro, do you want me to play louder or softer?” It was the perfect thing to say and it was said with great cleverness and A caricature of Arturo Toscanini by Enrico Caruso – all angles and oblique lines. diplomacy. Toscanini’s temper tantrums were famous throughout the world. The curious thing is that the musicians in his orchestras did not seem to take offense. They usually responded to these eruptions with calmness and understanding. But that made no difference to Toscanini. A raging temper, fortified with insults was his way of life. But there is a curious twist to this story. Toscanini was a raging, temperamental maestro, but only when at the podium. Off the podium he was the epitome of a calm gentleman. While conducting he demanded absolute perfection in music. But off the podium he became a shy, self-effacing mouse. If he went to a restaurant and the waiter brought him the wrong thing…he said...absolutely nothing! Buon appetito. articles.text: Copper Children, Midsummer Night’s Dream currently being shown The Oregon Shakespeare Festival, having cancelled its 2020 season due to Covid-19, is offering on-demand streaming service beginning with full-length plays from its 2020 season. The performances are accessible on laptops, tablets and mobile phones. This season’s offering has begun with The Copper Children by Karen Zacharias and is streaming from July 2-15. Zacharias previously wrote Destiny of Desire that won the Edgerton Foundation new play award and was featured as part of the 2018 season in Ashland. Copper Children is set in Arizona at the turn of the 20th century and is based on the true history of what was known as the orphan trains, a welfare program that sent predominantly Irish orphaned and homeless children from Eastern U.S. cities across the country to foster homes in the Midwest. Oregon Shakespeare Festival is also featuring the Shakespearian comedy, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, with music. It is streaming July 9-22. The productions are complete shows with a full cast of actors filmed on stage during their short runs earlier this year. The intent is to give patrons a live theater experience with the cameras having been placed directly in front of the stage, so the show is experienced as if you are sitting in a front row seat. The productions are handled by Uscreen, a provider of video-on-demand services. Subscribers will be able to access the play at a cost of $15 per show by setting up an account on the hosting site. Information can be found online by searching Oregon Shakespeare Festival or by e-mailing: streaming@osfashland.org Photo by Jenny Graham, Oregon Shakespeare Festival. articles.text: Reprinted from May 6, 2015. This cake will be the highlight of your summer brunch or tea time. It pulls together easily enough for kids and dads alike to prepare, yet has a simple elegance that fits this special occasion. I’ve added a hint of orange to the cake for that je ne sais quoi complement to the strawberries. Select perfectly ripe fruit to maximize the berries’ flavor. Medium-sized fruit is best for distribution on the cake and ease when it comes time to slice and serve. Helpful tip: Set a timer to track the initial 10 minutes of baking so you will know when to reduce the oven temperature. Reset the timer for 45 minutes to begin checking the cake to see if it done. Fresh Strawberry Cake Adapted from Martha Stewart INGREDIENTS • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened, plus additional for the pan • 1-1/ 2 cup all-purpose flour • 1-1/ 2 teaspoon baking powder • 1/ 2 teaspoon salt • 3/4 cup granulated sugar, preferably super-fine; plus an additional 2 tablespoons for topping • 1 large egg, room temperature • 1/4 cup whole milk, approx. • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1 medium orange • 1 pint fresh strawberries, approximately 16 berries; hulled and halved lengthwise INSTRUCTIONS Adjust oven rack to the lower 1/ 3 position in the oven and preheat to 350°F. Butter a 9-inch pie pan. Whisk together the flour, baking powder and salt in a small bowl. Set aside. Remove the zest of the orange using a microplane or very fine grater, avoiding the white pith. This yields about 1 teaspoon of zest. Set aside. Cut the orange in half and extract the juice into a measuring cup. This yields about 1/ 4 cup of juice. Add enough whole milk to bring the combined liquids to measure 1/ 2 cup total. Set aside. Put 6 tablespoons of butter and 3/ 4 cup of sugar into a large mixing bowl. Beat on medium-high speed until they become pale and fluffy, about 3 minutes. Reduce the mixer speed to medium low and add the egg, orange zest, vanilla and juice-milk mixture. It will look curdled. This is OK. Reduce mixer speed to low and gradually add the flour mixture. Mix until just incorporated, do not overmix. You can use a silicone spatula to combine the last bits of flour clinging to the bowl. Transfer the batter into the buttered pie pan, smoothing to level it with a spatula. Place the strawberries on top of the batter, cut sides down and close to each other but not overlapping. Sprinkle the remaining 2 tablespoons of sugar evenly over the berries. Bake the cake for 10 minutes, then reduce the oven temperature to 325° F. Bake until cake is golden and a toothpick inserted into the center of it comes out with only a few crumbs clinging to it, about 45-50 additional minutes. Remove from the oven and let cool on a wire rack. Cake may be served warm or at room temperature with a bit of whipped cream and sliced berries. For more information or to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok at PiedmontPantry.com.

articles.text: Whether you’re planning a refresh or a complete kitchen remodel, the first step is to examine your space. Take a moment to think about how you use and move throughout your kitchen. Kitchens are no longer just for cooking. Integrating dining and additional workspaces into your new kitchen can make it a multi-functional room. Including a workstation to make the kitchen the home’s command center will allow the family to work at home. Consider incorporating a casual space for dining via a counter or breakfast nook. Kitchen Remodel Taking Shape The next step is to determine the most functional use of space. Think about how the space works and any pain points you’d like to solve. There are three common kitchen layouts: U-shaped, I-shaped, and L-shaped kitchens. U-Shaped Kitchen This common kitchen layout is versatile, functional, and great for busy cooks. The workspace surrounds the cook for maximum efficiency and keeps everything within easy reach. This layout is also great for entertaining. I-Shaped Kitchen In this layout, the appliances are concentrated along a single wall. This simple kitchen design is great for small spaces and the biggest benefit is its cost effectiveness. However, the limited workspace of this kitchen layout can make it challenging for multiple cooks to operate at the same time. L-Shaped Kitchen This layout works best within a large kitchen footprint. It is the most ergonomically correct kitchen design and is perfect for a family with multiple chefs in the kitchen at the same time. Oftentimes, an island can be incorporated in the center of the kitchen for more workspace or casual dining. Kitchen Ergonomics Kitchen ergonomics should always factor into your design. Adding pull-out shelves in base cabinets make them more accessible and using open shelving gives you easy access to everyday items. Avid bakers may want a pop-up shelf for a KitchenAid mixer. Coffee drinkers will appreciate a station with a built-in espresso machine. Adding a wine cooler frees up refrigerator space and provides a high-end feel. All these elements can make a kitchen more comfortable and easier to work in. Merge Indoor and Outdoor Kitchens We are fortunate to live in the Bay Area with a mild climate year-round. One way to make your home feel more spacious and gain usable space is to integrate your indoor and outdoor spaces. Create a flow from your kitchen to your yard, patio, or balcony to maximize space. This creates space for entertaining and opportunities for a garden-to-table experience. Integrated accordion doors and no-threshold flooring erase the lines between indoors and outdoors. A complete guide for kitchen layout By Kevin Mond Whether you’re planning a refresh or a complete kitchen remodel, the first step is to examine your space. Take a moment to think about how you use and move throughout your kitchen. Kitchens are no longer just for cooking. Integrating dining and additional workspaces into your new kitchen can make it a multi-functional room. Including a workstation to make the kitchen the home’s command center will allow the family to work at home. Consider incorporating a casual space for dining via a counter or breakfast nook. Kitchen Remodel Taking Shape The next step is to determine the most functional use of space. Think about how the space works and any pain points you’d like to solve. There are three common kitchen layouts: U-shaped, I-shaped, and L-shaped kitchens. U-Shaped Kitchen This common kitchen layout is versatile, functional, and great for busy cooks. The workspace surrounds the cook for maximum efficiency and keeps everything within easy reach. This layout is also great for entertaining. I-Shaped Kitchen In this layout, the appliances are concentrated along a single wall. This simple kitchen design is great for small spaces and the biggest benefit is its cost effectiveness. However, the limited workspace of this kitchen layout can make it challenging for multiple cooks to operate at the same time. L-Shaped Kitchen This layout works best within a large kitchen footprint. It is the most ergonomically correct kitchen design and is perfect for a family with multiple chefs in the kitchen at the same time. Oftentimes, an island can be incorporated in the center of the kitchen for more workspace or casual dining. Kitchen Ergonomics Kitchen ergonomics should always factor into your design. Adding pull-out shelves in base cabinets make them more accessible and using open shelving gives you easy access to everyday items. Avid bakers may want a pop-up shelf for a KitchenAid mixer. The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Monday Reading Group opened July with a large turnout of 19 people on Monday, July 6. The group continues to meet virtually through Zoom technology. The July book selection, The Library Book by Susan Orlean, is a non-fiction account of the unsolved mystery of the most catastrophic library fire in American history. On the morning of April 29, 1986, a fire in the Los Angeles Main Public Library raged through its stacks. It reached 2000 degrees, burned for over seven hours, destroyed 400,000 books and damaged 700,000 more. The library was closed for seven years. An investigation into the cause of the fire led to the arrest of Harry Peak, a struggling actor who constantly changed his story about his activities during the day of the fire. His role in the fire remains a mystery, and its cause has never been conclusively determined. Peak was charged, but the evidence was not definitive and the charges were eventually dropped, after he countersued. Peak’s guilt or innocence was a question for the readers to discuss, and there was no consensus. While the fire and the story of Harry Peak provide the thread that weaves through the book, it is more than a fire mystery who-done-it. With a life-long love of books, Orlean fondly recalls the happy trips to her library that she had with her mother. Orlean expands the fire story and her personal experiences into a history of the Los Angeles Library, libraries more broadly, the city of Los Angeles, library staff, along with those who run and use libraries. The author shows us the larger role that libraries now play in our society, how they are more than just books. Many in the reading group loved the book. They appreciated how Orlean provided so much information about libraries, their history and the people associated with them. The author was also able to make an emotional connection with readers. Some could relate to Orlean’s library experiences and the library time she spent with her now declining mother. Some readers had similar library experiences when they were young. An interesting reader dynamic was the split between the women and men about the book. There were 16 women and three men in the group. All three men liked the book, though they did not have the level of passion for it that the women did. It was suggested that possibly young girls have more positive, emotional experiences with books and libraries than boys do. Participating in the discussion were: Rumi Ueno, Margie Blodgett, Jeri Lockhart, Sarah Johnson, Sally Arney, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Heidi Shale, Laura Goldman, Albert Chen, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Alicia Rivera, Bella Almanzan, Pat McSwain, Adriene Hamlin, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Carol Long and Priscilla Wanerus. Next came a discussion to select the next book to read. They had previously made The Black Swan by Nassim Nicholas Taleb and The Dutch House by Ann Patchett their August and September selections. However, with society’s current focus on racial justice, the group decided to read White Fragility by Robin DiAngelo for September. Assuming social distancing is still in place, the readers will meet again for a Zoom discussion on Monday, August 3 at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. articles.text: Book review by Ann P. McCauley The Perfume Collector by Kathleen Tessaro is a novel about the sensual awakening of two young women. It is set in glamorous Parisian apartments, stylish New York hotels, English country gardens in the spring, and warm, midnight beaches near Monte Carlo. Readers revel in descriptions of these lovely places before learning of an evil character who ends up on a dairy farm in Minnesota. One young woman is born to poverty but has extraordinary gifts that allow her to create a world of style and excitement that beguiles those around her. She flits around glamorous casinos in a shimmering dress and silver sandals, pausing in the doorway to catch the light. The other woman is an English debutante who complains that food with onions and garlic has too much flavor and who considers luxurious clothing garish. A French hairdresser turns her into a beauty, and a shop saleswoman puts her into a flattering Balenciaga “architecturally cut” dress. A charming, sensitive French man introduces her to…well…onions, garlic and other pleasures. Central to the novel is the appreciation, description, and enjoyment of the sense of smell. Fragrance, a character notes, is an aspiration. Perfume transports us from life as it is into a lovely place filled with our most sensually delicious moments, and so each person needs a perfume that reminds them of things they love – clean rain, jasmine in a flower garden, newly mown grass. It is a pleasure to spend time in the world of this novel. The Perfume Collector, Discovering Life Through the Senses, not the Mind, by Kathleen Tessaro. articles.text: Neil Guiney, a resident of Piedmont for 24 years, passed away peacefully at home in Oakland on May 7, 2020 after a brief struggle with cancer. Born Neil Terrence Guiney on February 14, 1945 in San Francisco, he was the son of Katherine Sullivan Guiney and Neil Joseph Guiney and a lifelong Bay Area resident. He was a member of the first graduating class of St. Francis High School in Mountain View. After graduating from St. Mary’s College in Moraga, he earned a Master’s Degree in English with an emphasis on Irish Theater from San Francisco State University in 1969. Upon completing his education in the arts, he became a carpenter, obtaining his General Contractors License in 1976. He married Julie Ann Fielder in 1973, and in 1979 they moved from San Francisco to Piedmont where they raised their two children. In 2003, they moved to Oakland, where they ultimately retired. As a builder he created beautiful homes, remodeling each of his houses to his exacting taste and specifications, just as he did for scores of clients over the years. His workshop in the garage was his favorite place to be, where he crafted furniture and worked on myriad projects. Neil was a Renaissance man at heart. He enjoyed playing many instruments throughout his life, from the piano to the fiddle. He loved literature, his vegetable garden, handwoven textiles and a wide variety of music and art. He spent many happy hours in museums throughout the world. In 2018, after a painstaking search of family records, Neil was very proud to obtain the necessary documentation that allowed him a dual citizenship in Ireland and the U.S. Though an avid 49ers and Warriors fan, his true love was the San Francisco Giants, a love he shared with his father. In 1958 Neil Guiney, a resident of Piedmont for 24 years, passed away on May 7. He was 75. articles.text: Julia Burke’s wildflower sidewalk strip in front of her house. As ongoing shelter-in-place takes its toll on daily life, many Piedmonters have found new and continued pleasure in their backyards. Just ask Eric Dam, manager of ACE Garden Center. “Everyone is gardening” Dam said. “They’re creating Victory Gardens. In the spring, we ran out of vegetable seeds. Now there’s a shortage of bark and soil, and our native plant supply clears out every week.” Julia Burke, a member of the Piedmont Garden Club and an avid native-plant gardener and beekeeper, is delighted to see more gardens springing up in town, especially with drought-tolerant and native species. She is hoping to see more city properties and sidewalk strips planted with wildflowers. “People need to know that native gardens can make a difference for wildlife and for drought,” she says. “These plants have evolved over thousands of years to withstand six months of drought. Non-natives don’t attract the insects that birds need to survive and feed their young. They need diversity. ‘The whole food web depends on natives, and it’s just as easy to grow them as non-natives,” she said. As the city’s Climate Challenge notes, replacing 1,000 sq. ft. of lawn with drought-tolerant plants can save up to 20,000 gallons of water a year. (See www. piedmontclimatechallenge.org/ action/replace-lawn.) Burke replaced the lawn in front of her house on LaSalle five years ago. Since then she has transformed the area into a hillside of colorful wildflowers including California poppies that reseed every year. Her fenced backyard is devoted to more wildflowers, vegetables, and beekeeping. She lets her lettuce, chard, and broccoli flower go to seed for the bees. This year, Burke planted all of her vegetables from seed and gave away six-packs of seedlings to friends. “Sunflowers are also a wonderful addition to attract birds and bees,” she said. “My yard is not landscaped, and I would never have anyone blowing it to disturb the leaves or the soil.” Burke’s interest in beekeeping began when she learned about it from Piedmonters Carter and Patty Dunlap (whose beekeeping and fruit tree garden will be featured in a future Climate Corner). “I thought I was allergic to bees,” Burke said, “but after getting stung a few times, I found I wasn’t allergic. It’s Zen-like to watch the bees coming and going.” Plus, they give her 30 pounds of honey a year – a pretty sweet deal.
